title: Chapter 55: Supreme Courage 5
content:
Chapter 55

Wei Wuxian paused for a moment before speaking up again. "Still, even if it was hibernating, four hundred years is a bit much, don't you think? You said this Xuanwu of Slaughter has an appetite for living humans—just how many people did it actually eat?"

Lan Wangji replied, "According to historical records, every time it surfaced, it consumed anywhere from two to three hundred people at minimum to the entire population of whole towns and villages at most. Across its several rampages, it devoured at least five thousand living souls."

"Oh," Wei Wuxian said, enlightened. "So it just gave itself a food coma."

The monster seemed fond of dragging its prey whole into its shell, likely hoarding them to snack on at its own pace. Maybe four centuries ago it had crammed its shell with far too many reserves in one go, and it simply hadn't finished digesting yet.

Lan Wangji ignored him. Undeterred, Wei Wuxian pressed on, "Speaking of food, have you ever practicedinedia? People like us can probably last three or four days without a bite to eat or a drop to drink. But if no rescue party shows up after that, our stamina, energy, and spiritual power are all going to take a nosedive."

If Wen Chao and his cronies had simply run for the hills and decided to wash their hands of the whole affair, that wouldn't be the worst outcome; hold out for three or four days, and reinforcements summoned by the other clans might arrive. The real fear was that the Wens wouldn't just sit on their hands—they’d actively kick them while they were down. After all, "the other clans" only meant the Gusu Lan and the Yunmeng Jiang. If the Wen Clan threw roadblocks in their way, that "three or four days" estimate would easily double.

Wei Wuxian retrieved a snapped branch and began sketching a rough map in the dirt, connecting a few crude lines. "The trip from Mount Muxi to Gusu is a little shorter than the trek back to Yunmeng, so your people ought to get here first. We just have to sit tight. Even if they don't make it, wait another day or two at most, and Jiang Cheng will have reached Lotus Pier. He’s sharp on his feet; the Wen guards won't be able to pin him down. There’s really nothing to worry about."

Lan Wangji kept his eyes cast downward, his posture worn and despondent. "No one is coming," he murmured softly.

Wei Wuxian blinked. "Hm?"

"The Cloud Recesses," Lan Wangji whispered, "has already burned."

Wei Wuxian probed carefully, "...Everyone made it out, right? Your uncle? Your brother?"

He had assumed that even if the Lan Clan Leader—Lan Wangji's father—was critically injured, Lan Qiren and Lan Xichen would still be there to steer the ship. Instead, Lan Wangji spoke in a wooden, hollow daze: "Father will not last much longer. Brother is missing."

The stick in Wei Wuxian's hand froze against the dirt.

Back on the mountain path, that disciple had mentioned the Lan Clan Leader was badly hurt. But he hadn't imagined it was dire enough to meanon the brink of death. It was very likely Lan Wangji had only just received the latest word over the past couple of days.

Even if the Lan Sect Leader had spent decades in secluded meditation, deaf to the outside world, a father was still a father. On top of that, Lan Xichen had vanished without a trace. No wonder Lan Wangji had been radiating such a suffocating, bitter edge today, his temper so easily frayed. An awkward lump formed in Wei Wuxian's throat; he had no idea what to say.

Then, turning his head without thinking, his entire body locked rigid.

The firelight washed over Lan Wangji’s profile like warm jade, throwing a crystal-clear gleam across the single tear track cutting down his cheek.

Wei Wuxian’s brain short-circuited.Holy hell.

A man like Lan Wangji probably shed tears only a handful of times in his entire life, and of all the rotten luck, Wei Wuxian had walked right into one of them. He had always been entirely helpless around crying people. When a woman cried, his immediate instinct was to swoop in, coax her, tease her, and do whatever it took to turn those tears into a smile. But a man’s tears were ten times worse. In his book, catching a dignified, unyielding man weeping was leagues more terrifying than accidentally walking in on a modest maiden taking a bath. And to make matters worse, he couldn't even offer a word of comfort.

Crushed under the weight of his ancestral home reduced to ash, his clan humiliated, his father dying, his brother missing, and his own body battered and broken—any platitude would ring painfully hollow.

Not knowing what to do with his hands, Wei Wuxian quickly averted his gaze. After an agonizing silence, he finally ventured, "Um... Lan Zhan."

Lan Wangji’s voice was pure frost: "Be quiet."

Wei Wuxian clamped his mouth shut.

A pocket of sap in the firewood popped with a sharp crack.

"Wei Ying," Lan Wangji murmured, his voice dead quiet. "You truly are... thoroughly vexing."

Wei Wuxian gave a subdued, "Oh..."

With everything crashing down on him,he thought,his head must be an absolute war zone, yet here I am, dancing in front of his face like a nuisance. No wonder he’s so furious. His leg is wrecked, so he doesn't have the strength to beat me black and blue—he had to settle for taking a chunk out of my arm instead... I'd better just give him some space.

After suffocating on his own thoughts for a while, he couldn't resist speaking up anyway. "I really wasn't trying to get on your nerves... I just wanted to ask if you're cold. The clothes dried by the fire. You take the inner robe; I'll keep the outer layer."

The inner robe was worn directly against the skin, making it somewhat improper to offer Lan Wangji his personal undergarment. But his outer robe was so caked in grime and gore it was unfit for human eyes. The people of Gusu Lan were notoriously fastidious about cleanliness; handing him that stained rag would feel downright insulting. Lan Wangji said nothing, nor did he look his way. Wei Wuxian gently set the dry, white inner robe beside him, slung the damp outer robe over his own shoulders, and quietly rolled out of the alcove to give him peace.

The two of them waited for three whole days.

Deep inside the subterranean cave, there was no sun or moon to mark the hours. The only reason they knew three days had passed was thanks to the Lan Clan’s terrifyingly rigid internal clock: falling asleep on the dot at nine and snapping awake at five without fail. All Wei Wuxian had to do was count how many naps Lan Wangji took to tally the days.

After three days of uninterrupted rest, the wound on Lan Wangji’s leg had stabilized, slowly on the mend, and he soon resumed his seated meditation to circulate his spiritual energy.

Wei Wuxian had made a conscious effort to stay out of his hair during this time. Once Lan Wangji regained his composure and reinhabited that deadpan, unreadable mask, Wei Wuxian sauntered back as if nothing had ever happened. He shamelessly played dumb, pretending he hadn't seen or heard a single thing that night, and made sure not to push his luck teasing him. Their dynamic settled into a quiet, neutral truce.

Over those days, they crept toward the black pool multiple times to scout the beast. The Xuanwu of Slaughter had dragged every last corpse into its shell; the colossal, pitch-black carapace floated on the water's surface like an impenetrable war galleon. During the first few trips, heavy, wet crunching echoed from within; later on, the chewing stopped, replaced by a rhythmic, subterranean snore that rumbled like muffled thunder.

They had toyed with the idea of slipping beneath the surface while the monster slept to locate the underwater escape tunnel, but staying submerged for barely half an incense stick was enough to stir the beast. And despite searching several times, they never caught sight of the tunnel Jiang Cheng had described. Wei Wuxian suspected it was being blocked by the creature’s bulk, but when he tried to bait it out of the water again, the monster seemed utterly lethargic after its feast, stubbornly refusing to budge.

They scoured the shores and gathered all the discarded arrows, longbows, and branding irons left behind by the Wen disciples. Dragging their haul back, they counted over a hundred arrows, more than thirty bows, and a dozen iron brands.

By then, the fourth day had arrived.

Lan Wangji picked up a longbow with his left hand, inspecting the grain and tensile strength of the stave. His right fingers caught the string and gave it a sharp pluck, releasing a crisp, ringing metallic twang.

These were proper weapons crafted by prominent cultivation clans for night-hunting fierce beasts; the materials used for both bow and string were far from ordinary. Lan Wangji unstrung every single bow, knotting the cords end-to-end to fashion one continuous, seamless cord. Gripping both ends, he snapped the line taut and gave it a vicious flick. The cord shot forward like a white whip of lightning; with a brilliant crack of light, a boulder ten paces away was blasted into powder.

Lan Wangji snapped his wrist, reeling the cord back as it cleaved through the air with a piercing shriek.

Wei Wuxian blinked. "The Chord Murder technique?"

Chord Murder was one of the Gusu Lan Clan's closely guarded secret arts, pioneered and passed down by Lan Yi, granddaughter of the founding ancestor Lan An and the clan's third-generation leader. Lan Yi was also the sole female clan leader in Gusu Lan's history. She walked the path of the zither; her instrument bore seven strings that could be detached and reassembled in an instant. Those seven silk cords, tapering from thick to hair-thin, could play pristine, ethereal hymns beneath her soft, pale fingers one moment, and slice through bone and flesh like warm butter the next—transforming into deadly slaughtering wire.

Lan Yi had originally engineered Chord Murder to assassinate clan rivals, earning her no small amount of controversy. Even the Lan Clan themselves held a conflicted view of her legacy. Yet no one could deny that Chord Murder remained the most devastating, lethal offensive technique in the Gusu Lan arsenal, equally terrifying at range or point-blank.

Lan Wangji said, "We breach it from within."

The shell was a fortress, its exterior scales as tough as tempered plate, virtually impenetrable. But the harder the outer shell, the softer and more fragile the fleshy anatomy hidden inside was bound to be. Wei Wuxian had mulled over the exact same theory over the past few days.

More than that, he understood their current predicament. After three days of recuperating, their stamina and spiritual energy were peaking right now. If they dragged this out any longer, their strength would only decline. The fourth day was drawing to a close, and rescue had yet to show.

Rather than sitting around waiting to die, gambling everything on a desperate offensive was their only shot. If they could bring down this Xuanwu of Slaughter together, they could escape through the submerged cave beneath the pool.

Wei Wuxian agreed, "I’m with you on breaking it from the inside. But I know a thing or two about your family's Chord Murder. Operating inside that cramped shell will tie your hands, giving you no room to maneuver. Add your fractured leg to the mix, and your mobility will be cut in half."

It was the cold, hard truth, and Lan Wangji knew it. Both of them understood that playing the hero and taking on a task beyond your physical limits did nothing except drag everyone down with you.

Wei Wuxian smiled. "Leave it to me."

A low crescent of the Xuanwu of Slaughter's shell still bobbed above the dark pool.

Its four clawed limbs, head, and tail were tucked away inside. A gaping opening gaped at the front, flanked by five smaller apertures along the sides and rear. It resembled a desolate island or an eroded hill—black, jagged, carpeted in thick moss and draped in slimy, dark tangles of lake weed.

Without a sound, a bundle of arrows and iron brands strapped securely to his back, Wei Wuxian slipped through the water like a slender silver fish, surfacing right in front of the main opening.

The lower half of the aperture was submerged, allowing him to swim right inside. Passing the entrance, he hauled himself up into the cavern of the shell. His boots sank into what felt like a thick, foul soup of rotting mud, drenched in stagnant water. The stench that crashed over him was so suffocating he almost choked out a curse.

It was a putrid mix of rot and sickly-sweet gore, instantly reminding him of a bloated dead rat he’d once fished out of a lake back in Yunmeng. He clamped a hand over his nose, grimacing.Good grief... Thank heavens I didn't let Lan Zhan crawl in here. With his pristine, untouchable sensibilities, one whiff of this garbage would have made him vomit on the spot. If he didn't throw up, he'd pass out cold from the fumes.

The beast snored with slow, rhythmic rumblings. Wei Wuxian held his breath, creeping forward as his boots sank deeper with every step. After three strides, the muck was lapping at his knees. Submerged beneath the slime were hard, jagged lumps. Bending low, his fingers swept through the filth—only to brush against something soft and tangled.

Hair. Human hair.

Wei Wuxian recoiled his hand. He knew full well these were the remains dragged inside by the monster. Probing a little further, his fingertips grazed a boot; the half-eaten leg wedged inside had decayed into a mush of rancid meat and yellow bone.

It seemed this beast had terrible table manners. Leftovers it hadn't finished, or cuts it hadn't gotten around to swallowing, simply dripped from between its fangs, spat carelessly onto the floor of its shell. Over centuries of feeding, the refuse had piled into a thick layer of sediment. And right now, Wei Wuxian was wading through a literal swamp of liquefied human remains.

Having tumbled through dirt and blood for the past few days, his robes were already ruined beyond recognition, so adding a little more filth hardly mattered. He wiped his palms on his trousers and pushed deeper.

The snores grew thunderous, each exhalation blowing a wave of hot, stagnant air across the chamber, while the layer of corpse sludge rose higher against his thighs. Finally, his outstretched fingers brushed against rough, uneven skin. Tracing the flesh upward, he mapped out the anatomy: the head and neck were plated in armor, followed by thick, cratered hide that gradually grew thinner, softer, and more delicate the deeper it went toward the belly.

By now, the sludge was up to his waist. The bodies here hadn't been picked clean yet, preserved in large, recognizable chunks; calling it sludge was generous—it was an abattoir pile. Wei Wuxian reached over his shoulder to untie the bundle of arrows and brands, only to find the irons snagged on something buried in the heap.

He gripped the shaft of a branding iron, hauling backward with all his might. The metal tore free with a muffled scrape, dragging an object out from the pile with a faint, metallicclang.

Wei Wuxian froze solid.

He held his breath for several seconds. When no movement followed and the snores continued uninterrupted, he let out a soundless sigh of relief.That iron caught on something buried in the bodies. Sounded like metal, didn't it? And long, too. Let's see if it's useful—I'm desperately short on weapons. A high-grade spiritual sword would be a godsend right about now!

Reaching out into the dark, his fingers closed around the object. It was long, heavy, utterly blunt, its surface crusted in thick layers of rust.

The very instant his skin made contact, a chorus of shrieks detonated inside his skull!

It was an agonizing wall of sound—tens of thousands of voices wailing in shredded, hopeless torment. An icy shockwave crawled up his arm, instantly freezing his marrow. Wei Wuxian flinched, violently snatching his hand back.What the hell is that?! The resentment clinging to it is monstrous!

Suddenly, the pitch-black cavern lit up. A faint, reddish-gold amber glow illuminated his surroundings, casting Wei Wuxian's silhouette across the dark expanse—and revealing a pitch-black iron sword buried in the heap ahead. In the shadow cast against the wall, the blade was angled directly through his silhouette’s heart.

This was deep inside the beast's shell. Where was light coming from?

Wei Wuxian whipped around. Sure enough, a massive pair of golden orbs was staring down at him from inches away.

The thunderous snoring had stopped completely. That eerie amber light was spilling directly from the Xuanwu’s pupils!

The beast bared its jagged, black-and-yellow tusks, letting loose an earth-shattering roar.

Standing right before its maw, the concussive acoustic shockwave hit Wei Wuxian point-blank, nearly rupturing his eardrums and sending a jolt of bruised agony through his chest. Seeing the massive jaws snap shut toward him, he shoved the tied bundle of iron brands horizontally into its mouth. The timing and angle were immaculate—the rigid iron rods jammed between its upper and lower palate, wedging its jaws open!

Seizing the opening while its mouth was locked, Wei Wuxian slammed a bundle of arrows straight into the thinnest patch of skin beneath its throat. The wooden shafts were slender, but bound in tight clusters of five, they punched deep into the soft flesh, driven all the way to the fletchings like a cluster of venomous needles. Driven mad by the sudden agony, the Xuanwu clamped its jaws shut with monstrous force, crumpling the iron rods like twigs, bending the straight metal into warped hooks under its sheer bite force. Wei Wuxian plunged several more bundles into its soft underbelly. Having never suffered such agony since its birth, the beast lost its mind; its serpentine neck thrashed violently inside the shell, slamming its skull against the interior walls. The mountain of corpses tossed like a stormy sea, triggering an avalanche of rotting limbs that nearly buried Wei Wuxian alive.

The monster’s eyes burned wild with savage fury as its jaws stretched impossibly wide, inhaling like an abyss. A torrential slide of bodies rushed toward its throat; struggling against the current, Wei Wuxian’s hand caught the hilt of the rusted iron sword. A sudden chill gripped his chest as the wailing shrieks flooded his ears once more.

His legs were already being dragged into the creature’s open maw. As the jaws prepared to snap shut, he leveraged the rusted sword, repeating his earlier trick and wedging the heavy steel vertically between its upper and lower palates.

The digestive tract of a centurions-old beast was notoriously corrosive; swallow a living human, and they’d be dissolved into acidic vapor in seconds!

Wei Wuxian held the iron sword with an iron grip, acting like a jagged bone lodged in its throat, refusing to slide down or yield. The Xuanwu slammed its skull repeatedly against the shell, unable to swallow the stubborn splinter keeping its mouth pried open, yet refusing to spit it out. In a frenzy, it burst outward!

Terrorized by the relentless stabs inside its own shell, it scrambled to escape its own armor, violently shoving its serpentine neck and upper torso out through the front aperture, exposing the tender, unprotected flesh of its throat to the open air. Lan Wangji had already rigged his chord across the lip of the shell, waiting for this exact moment. The instant the neck burst through, he snapped the line taut, plucking the cord with a vicious flick that sent the vibrating wire sawing deep into the meat!

Trapped between the two of them, the beast could neither advance nor retreat. It was a malformed monster, not a true divine beast, possessing barely a shred of higher intellect; pushed past the brink by agonizing pain, it went completely berserk. Whipping its head and lashing its tail, it thrashed wildly through the black pool, churning the water into a colossal whirlpool that threw up towering waves. Yet no matter how violently it fought, one boy remained wedged like an anchor in its throat, keeping its jaws locked, while the other relentlessly tightened the chord around its exposed neck, sawing inward millimeter by millimeter. The cut ground deeper; the water ran redder!

Lan Wangji held the cord with an unyielding grip, refusing to ease the tension for a fraction of a second, holding the line for three grueling hours.

Only after three agonizing hours did the Xuanwu of Slaughter’s thrashing slowly grind to a halt.

Its vital throat tissue had been severed so deeply by the chord that its head was nearly detached from its torso. Having poured everything into maintaining that crushing tension, Lan Wangji’s palms were shredded, slick with blood and scored by deep wire-burns. The massive shell drifted limp atop the pool, the dark water dyed a vivid, muddy purple, reeking of gore like an infernal slaughterhouse.

With a heavy splash, Lan Wangji dove into the pool, swimming toward the serpentine head. The monster’s golden eyes remained wide open, though the pupils had blown wide and vacant, its fangs still locked in a stubborn, dying clench.

Lan Wangji called out, "Wei Ying!"

Not a sound escaped the beast's jaws.

Lan Wangji reached out, clamping his bloody fingers around the upper and lower tusks, wrenching them apart with everything he had left. Treading water made it difficult to find purchase; it took several grueling seconds to pry the jaws open. Wedged inside was the blackened iron sword, its tip and hilt driven deep into the creature's palate and tongue, the heavy blade warped into an extreme curve under the crushing pressure.

Curled tightly into a ball, Wei Wuxian hung limply inside, his forehead resting on his knees, his hands still white-knuckling the blunt edge of the blade, inches from slipping down the monster's gullet. Lan Wangji seized his collar, hauling him out into the open air. The moment the jaws separated, the rusted sword slipped free, sinking into the dark depths of the pool.

Eyes shut tight, Wei Wuxian slumped bonelessly against his chest, an arm draped over Lan Wangji’s shoulder. Lan Wangji locked an arm around his waist, keeping them afloat in the crimson water. "Wei Ying!"

His hand trembled faintly. He was just reaching out to touch Wei Wuxian's cheek when the boy gasped, jolting awake like he’d been struck by lightning. "What happened?! Did it drop?! Is it dead?!"

He thrashed instinctively, nearly dragging both of them beneath the surface. Lan Wangji tightened his grip on his waist, steadying them. "It is dead!"

Wei Wuxian’s eyes were vacant and unfocused, his thoughts struggling to string together. After a long beat, he mumbled, "Dead? It's dead... Good! It's dead. The damn thing wouldn't stop shrieking... rolling around... knocked me clean out. Oh, right—the tunnel! The underwater tunnel, let's move. We have to get out through the tunnel."

Noticing his disjointed cadence, Lan Wangji murmured, "What is wrong with you?"

Wei Wuxian forced a burst of energy, waving a hand. "Nothing! Let's get out of here, time is wasting."

Time was indeed of the essence. Lan Wangji gave a slight nod. "I will guide you."

"No need, I can—" Lan Wangji’s arm remained clamped around his waist like an iron vice, brooking no argument: "Breathe in."

Diving in such a dazed state was practically begging for disaster. Wei Wuxian wasn't about to argue. Ignoring the foul, blood-soaked water, both drew a deep breath and plunged beneath the surface.

Moments later, two splashes broke the purple ripples as they resurfaced.

Wei Wuxian spat a mouthful of bloody water, wiping his face only to smear more crimson across his cheeks, looking utterly disheveled. "What the hell?! Where is the tunnel?!"

Jiang Cheng had sworn there was an underwater fissure wide enough for five or six people to swim through at once, and the other disciples had definitely escaped through it. Wei Wuxian had assumed the beast's bulk was simply obscuring the opening earlier, but now that the carcass had shifted, the area where it had been nesting was bare stone.

Water dripped from Lan Wangji’s soaked hair. He said nothing. Their eyes met, and the same chilling realization struck them both.

During its death throes, the monster’s violent thrashing and clawing had collapsed the subterranean rock, or its massive shell had crushed the opening shut. The only escape route... was completely caved in.

Wei Wuxian broke Lan Wangji’s grip, diving back under the surface, with Lan Wangji following right behind. They searched every inch of the flooded rock face, but found nothing. Not even a crevice wide enough for a hand to slip through.

Wei Wuxian surfaced, gasping, "What do we do now?"

After a heavy pause, Lan Wangji replied, "We return to shore first."

Wei Wuxian rubbed his face, exhausted. "...Right. Back to shore."

Completely spent, they dragged themselves to the rocky bank, their robes dripping with dark purple muck. Wei Wuxian stripped off his outer robe, wringing out the water and snapping the fabric in frustration. "Are you kidding me?! We took on that monster because we were running out of time and wouldn't have the strength to fight it if we waited any longer. We finally kill the damn bastard, and the son of a bitch caves the exit in! Fuck!"

Hearing that curse, Lan Wangji’s brow twitched. He opened his mouth to chide him, but thought better of it and held his tongue.

Wei Wuxian snapped his robe again, muttering curses, when his knees suddenly buckled. Lan Wangji darted forward, catching him by the elbows. Leaning heavily against him, Wei Wuxian breathed, "I'm fine, I'm fine... Just out of gas. Oh, right, Lan Zhan—did you see that sword I was holding in its mouth? Where did it go?"

"It sank to the bottom," Lan Wangji replied. "Why?"

"Sank? Ah, forget it then."

Back when his hands were locked around that hilt, that torrential wall of shrieks had echoed non-stop in his ears, chilling his bones and making his vision swim. That sword was undeniably something extraordinary. The Xuanwu had devoured at least five thousand people, and when it dragged them into its shell whole, plenty must have still been breathing. That heavy blade was likely the spiritual weapon of some fallen cultivator swallowed centuries ago. Buried in that mountain of corpses for four hundred years, it had marinated in the concentrated agony and dark malice of thousands of living and dead souls, drinking in their final screams.

Wei Wuxian had intended to inspect the iron properly, but since it had plunged to the bottom and they were trapped down here anyway, bringing it up would only serve to stir up an argument with Lan Wangji. He waved a dismissive hand, sighing inwardly,Not a single damn thing is going right today.

He dragged his boots forward, Lan Wangji trailing silently at his heel. Two steps later, Wei Wuxian’s knees gave out again.

Lan Wangji caught him once more. This time, he pressed a cool palm flat against Wei Wuxian’s forehead. After a beat, he murmured, "Wei Ying... you are burning."

Wei Wuxian reached up, resting his hand against Lan Wangji’s brow. "You feel pretty warm yourself."

Lan Wangji gently brushed his hand away, his tone flat. "Your hands are like ice."

Wei Wuxian blinked sluggishly. "Guess my head is a little fuzzy..."

Four or five days ago, he’d dumped all the crushed herbs from Mianmian’s sachet onto Lan Wangji’s fractured leg, settling for a cursory wipe across his own scorched chest. Deprived of proper rest, diving into a soup of rancid corpses and filthy water had finally triggered a violent infection.

Wei Wuxian had come down with a blazing fever.

Pushing forward for a few more steps, the vertigo grew overwhelming; unable to lift his boots, he slumped straight onto the dirt, murmuring in confusion, "How did I get a fever this easily? I haven't been sick in years."

Lan Wangji declined to comment on the phrase "this easily." He said simply, "Lie down."

Wei Wuxian complied, slumping onto his back. Lan Wangji took his hand, steadily channeling spiritual energy into his meridians.

After lying still for a minute, Wei Wuxian sat back up. Lan Wangji said, "Lie still."

Pulling his hand back, Wei Wuxian muttered, "Save your energy. You barely have enough left for yourself."

Lan Wangji took his wrist again, repeating firmly, "Lie still."

Days ago, Lan Wangji had been the helpless one, subjected to Wei Wuxian’s teasing and fussing; today the tables had turned, and Wei Wuxian had no choice but to let himself be handled.

Yet even flat on his back, Wei Wuxian was incapable of staying quiet. Before long, he started grumbling, "It hurts. The ground is too hard."

"What do you want?"

"To lie somewhere else."

Lan Wangji looked around the barren cave. "Where else do you expect to lie right now?"

Wei Wuxian grinned weakly. "Lend me your lap."

Lan Wangji’s face remained an unmoving stone. "Stop fooling around."

"I'm serious! My head is spinning. It's not like you're a maiden—what's there to be afraid of?"

"Even if I am not a maiden, you cannot simply recline wherever you please."

Seeing his brow furrow, Wei Wuxian groaned, "I'm not fooling around, you're the one being difficult! I don't get it, Lan Zhan—why are you always like this?"

"Like what?"

Wei Wuxian rolled onto his stomach, resting his chin on his crossed arms. "Everyone else pretends to find me annoying while secretly liking me deep down, but with you, you never have a good look for me. We've literally bled for each other down here, and you won't even lend me your leg to rest my head on? Always lecturing me... Are you seventy years old?"

Lan Wangji replied coolly, "The fever has made you delirious."

Perhaps the fever truly had scrambled his wits, because before long, Wei Wuxian drifted off.

In his dreams, the bed felt surprisingly comfortable—as if his head really was resting on someone's lap, a cool, soothing hand laid gently across his burning forehead. It felt so pleasant that he tossed and rolled around happily, and no one scolded him for it. When he rolled off onto the dirt, someone gently patted his hair, gathered him up, and settled his head back onto that soft lap.

Yet when his eyes cracked open, he was still sprawled on the cold stone floor. At most, someone had tucked a neat pile of dry leaves beneath the back of his head, offering a modest cushion. Lan Wangji sat a healthy distance away, having stoked a fresh fire that washed over his features like warm, elegant jade.

Wei Wuxian sighed inwardly.A dream, obviously.

With their self-engineered escape route collapsed, the two were stranded in the cavern, left with no choice but to pin their hopes on the Yunmeng Jiang Clan’s rescue. Another two days crawled by. Throughout those forty-eight hours, Wei Wuxian drifted in and out of a low-grade fever, cycling between restless sleep and groggy wakefulness. Only Lan Wangji’s steady, intermittent infusions of spiritual energy kept his condition from spiraling out of control.

"Ah... so bored."

"Seriously, so bored."

"It's too quiet."

"Aaaah—"

"I'm starving. Lan Zhan, go chop up some of that turtle meat for dinner."

"Never mind, forget I said that. A human-eating monster's meat probably tastes like rot. You stay put."

"Lan Zhan, why are you like this? You're so dull. Lips sealed, eyes shut, won't talk to me, won't look at me... What are you, a meditating monk? Oh, right—your founding ancestor was an actual monk. I forgot."

Lan Wangji’s voice broke the silence: "Quiet. You are burning. Do not speak. Conserve your strength."

Wei Wuxian perked up. "You finally answered! How many days have we been waiting? Why hasn't anyone come to pull us out yet?"

"Not even a single full day has passed."

Wei Wuxian threw an arm over his eyes, groaning, "Why does time drag this badly? It has to be because I'm stuck with you. If only it were Jiang Cheng down here—trading insults with him would be ten times more entertaining than this. Jiang Cheng! Where the hell did you die?! It's been nearly a week!!!"

Lan Wangji poked the firewood with a branch, the strike carrying an accidental flick of sharp sword intent that sent sparks swirling into the air like wild embers. He said coldly, "Rest."

Curling into a ball, his face turned toward the fire, Wei Wuxian whined, "Are you serious? I literally just opened my eyes and you're telling me to sleep again. Do you hate seeing me awake that much?"

Withdrawing the branch, Lan Wangji replied with pristine poise, "You are overthinking."

Wei Wuxian scoffed inwardly:Impenetrable. He was way more fun a few days ago when his face was darker than the bottom of a wok, barking at me with actual inflection and biting my arm when he lost his temper. Though catching Lan Zhan like that was a once-in-a-lifetime miracle; I doubt I'll ever see it again.

He pressed, "I'm dying of boredom. Lan Zhan, chat with me. You pick the topic."

"What hour do you usually retire?"

Wei Wuxian rolled his eyes. "What a dreadfully dry topic. It makes me totally unmotivated to answer. But out of respect for you, I'll bite: back at Lotus Pier, I never go to sleep before two in the morning. Half the time, I pull all-nighters."

Lan Wangji frowned. "Improper. A foul habit."

"Do you think everyone lives by your family's monk rules?"

"It must be corrected."

Wei Wuxian clapped his hands over his ears. "I'm an invalid! I'm burning up with a fever, Lan-er-gege—can't you say something nice? Coax this poor, pitiful patient a little?"

Lan Wangji fell silent.

Wei Wuxian sighed, "Can't do it? Fine, I figured. Well, if you won't talk, can you sing? How about a song?"

It was a completely flippant remark, tossed out purely to bicker and kill time; he had zero expectation of an answer. Yet after an agonizing silence, a low, exquisitely gentle melody began echoing softly through the hollow vastness of the cavern.

Lan Wangji was actually singing.

Wei Wuxian closed his eyes, rolling onto his back, splaying his limbs out with a relaxed sigh. "That's lovely."

He murmured, "What is the name of this song?"

Lan Wangji seemed to whisper a quiet phrase under his breath. Wei Wuxian cracked an eye open. "What was that?"
